item.title: Discovery and Clinical Development of Ceperognastat, a Low-Dose, CNS-Penetrant O -Linked N -Acetylglucosaminidase Inhibitor
item.description:
Abstract
Postmortem brain examinations in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) reveal β-amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles resulting from tau protein aggregation, and neuronal and synaptic loss, which collectively impair brain function. O-linked N-acetylglucosami‐nidase (OGA) is an enzyme that removes O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) from proteins including tau. In animal tauopathy models, OGA inhibition was shown to increase O-GlcNAc−tau levels, leading to reduced tau hyperphosphorylation and aggregation. These results inspired efforts to develop OGA inhibitors for the treatment of AD and tauopathies. Here we report the discovery and clinical development of ceperognastat (LY3372689), a low-dose, CNS-penetrant OGA inhibitor that has been evaluated in a completed phase II study in patients with early symptomatic AD.

item.title: Discovery of Pan-KRAS Inhibitor GNE-6226: Harnessing an Aminopyridine Pharmacophore to Broadly Target KRAS Mutants
item.description:
Abstract
RAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer, yet limited treatments are available for patients with mutations beyond KRAS G12C. While pan-RAS inhibitors have entered the clinic to benefit a broader population of patients harboring RAS mutations, we sought to develop pan-KRAS inhibitors (selective for KRAS over HRAS and NRAS) that may offer an improved therapeutic index. Herein, we describe the discovery of GNE-6226, a pan-KRAS inhibitor exhibiting exquisite potency across a range of KRAS mutants. Using a structure-based design, we transitioned from mutant-selective inhibitors to a pan-KRAS inhibition profile, identifying the aminopyridine headgroup as a crucial motif. This headgroup establishes key ligand−protein interactions with conserved residues within the switch-II pocket while avoiding steric clashes with KRAS mutants. We present extensive cellular and in vivo profiling of GNE-6226, highlighting its robust MAPK pathway modulation and tumor growth inhibition in vivo across G12V- and G12D-mutant xenograft mouse models.

item.title: Ferrous Ion-Activatable Thiol-Selective Covalent-Reversible Electrophiles to Enhance Erastin-Induced Ferroptosis
item.description:
Abstract
Ferroptosis is a unique form of cell death and characterized by the ferrous ion-based Fenton reaction to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) of lipid. However, ferroptosis could be inhibited by biothiols (i.e., GSH) because of their antioxidant function. Herein, we report a ferrous ion-activatable thiol-selective covalent electrophile to enhance Erastin-induced ferroptosis. This activatable electrophile containing a key pharmacophore of the endoperoxide bond remained caged and did not react with biothiols until it was activated by a ferrous ion to generate a highly reactive Michael acceptor, 1, 2-diacetylethylene. Notably, the activated thiol-selective electrophile reacted with thiols in a reversible covalent manner. Finally, a compound library of activatable electrophiles was constructed, generating a lead compound (17h) that did not inhibit cell growth but enhanced the Erastin-induced ferroptosis. Together, this study provides not only a novel mechanism to design activatable covalent electrophiles but also a unique covalent reversible ligand showing high reactivity and specificity toward biothiols.

item.title: Dual Inhibitors of Brain Carbonic Anhydrases and Cholinesterases Protect against Amyloid-β-Induced Neurotoxicity and Improve Cognitive Function in Mice
item.description:
Abstract
This work introduces tacrine-based multitarget ligands inhibiting brain carbonic anhydrases (CAs) and cholinesterases (ChEs) for targeting distinct yet interrelated pathological aspects of Alzheimer’s disease (AD): cholinergic dysfunction and amyloid-β-induced neurovascular, oxidative, and inflammatory stress. Modular optimization identified a subset of compounds inhibiting target CAs with KI values of 1.6−89.6 nM and cholinesterases with IC50 values of 0.53−113 nM. In silico simulations confirmed dual-target binding with retention of canonical interactions and formation of complementary stabilizing contacts. In RA−SH−SY5Y cells exposed to oligomeric amyloid-β, selected compounds effectively reduced cytotoxicity and reactive oxygen species production while preserving mitochondrial integrity. In a mouse social recognition memory model, dual inhibitors enhanced memory retention up to 48 h, outperforming the single-target approach. This work identifies dual CA/ChE inhibition as a promising complementary strategy for AD and related disorders: CA inhibition mitigates Aβ-induced oxidative, inflammatory, and neurovascular stress, whilst ChE inhibition supports cholinergic neurotransmission and memory consolidation.

item.title: Probing Different Chain Lengths and Saturation of the Fatty Acid Tail on Triglyceride-Mimetic Ionizable Lipids-Mediated siRNA Delivery
item.description:
Abstract
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are regarded as a promising delivery vehicle for small interfering RNA (siRNA) for the treatment of acute liver failure. However, current LNPs show suboptimal lysosomal escape ability and biodegradability. Monoglycerides used as co-lipids show excellent lysosomal escape ability and biodegradability. However, they lack ionizable heads and only have a single hydrophobic tail. Accordingly, we design and synthesize five new triglyceride-mimetic ionizable lipids featuring variable fatty acid tail lengths and saturation levels, derived from triglyceride-like ionizable lipids that have two fatty acid tails and a tertiary amine. The ionizable lipids are susceptible to lipase-mediated degradation, thereby enhancing the biosafety of LNPs. Notably, among the synthetic lipids, 3-TG-OA displays distinct advantages in cellular internalization, lysosomal escape, biodistribution, and gene silencing efficacy. Our findings provide novel insights into the structure−activity relationship of fatty acid tails and establish a robust non-viral delivery platform for siRNA delivery.

item.title: A Mitochondria-Targeted CPI-613 Derivative Overcomes Gemcitabine Resistance and Reduces Hepatic Metastasis in Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Gemcitabine-resistant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) can acquire an oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-high phenotype, creating a therapeutically exploitable vulnerability. Here, we developed compound 17, a triphenylphosphonium-conjugated CPI-613 derivative that suppresses pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) activity and mitochondrial respiration. By perturbing oxidative metabolism and redox homeostasis, 17 induced mitochondrial dysfunction and ferroptotic cell death, with PANC-1-GemR cells displaying greater sensitivity than parental PANC-1 cells. This selectivity translated in vivo: 17 outperformed gemcitabine in resistant xenografts and dose-dependently suppressed syngeneic Panc02 tumors. Compound 17 also attenuated EMT-associated phenotypes and hepatic metastatic burden without overt toxicity. These findings identify OXPHOS dependence as an actionable vulnerability in drug-resistant PDAC and position 17 as a promising mitochondria-targeted candidate for treating PDAC and limiting hepatic metastasis.

item.title: Discovery of First-in-Class hCA II/ROCK Dual Inhibitors with Both IOP-Lowering and Retinal Neuroprotective Activities for the Treatment of Glaucoma
item.description:
Abstract
Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Current first-line therapies frequently yield suboptimal intraocular pressure (IOP) control. Furthermore, many patients develop progressive visual field loss despite adequate pressure management. To address this gap, we developed a class of first-in-class dual-target inhibitors against carbonic anhydrase II (CA II) and Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase (ROCK). Among them, A3 showed 6250-fold higher hCA II inhibitory potency than the initial fragment with favorable selectivity and 1.2-/1.7-fold higher ROCK1/2 inhibitory activity than fasudil. In vivo, A3 produced potent and sustained IOP reduction across multiple models. Notably, in the DBA/2J spontaneous glaucoma model, it potently lowered IOP and preserved retinal structural integrity. Meanwhile, A3 attenuated retinal ganglion cell apoptosis via its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, thereby conferring optic neuroprotection with favorable systemic safety. Overall, A3 overcomes key limitations of current antiglaucoma drugs and represents a promising candidate for combined IOP-lowering and optic neuroprotective therapy.

item.title: Discovery of Potent and Selective Quinazoline-Based LATS1/2 Inhibitors Promoting Hepatic Regeneration
item.description:
Abstract
Therapeutic acceleration of endogenous liver regeneration remains a considerable unmet need for patients with acute or chronic liver injury. Among the pathways that coordinate regenerative responses, the Hippo pathway and its main components LATS1/2 kinases play a critical role by limiting YAP-dependent transcriptional programs associated with regeneration. Pharmacological inhibition of LATS1/2 thus represents a strategy to activate hepatic YAP signaling and promote tissue repair. Herein, we report the discovery of quinazoline-based LATS1/2 inhibitors derived from VT-02956 (1). Structure−activity relationship studies identified compound 24, a single-digit nanomolar LATS1/2 inhibitor with improved cellular YAP activation and metabolic stability. Compound 24 showed favorable kinase selectivity (S(35) = 0.04) and improved pharmacokinetics. In a partial hepatectomy mouse model, intraperitoneal administration of 24 activated YAP signaling, as evidenced by the upregulation of Cyr61 and Ankrd1, and significantly enhanced hepatocyte proliferation. These findings establish a medicinal chemistry foundation for developing LATS1/2 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for hepatic regeneration.

item.title: Isotopic Labeling of the Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Binimetinib with Fluorine-18 and Preclinical Evaluation
item.description:
Abstract
The Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK signaling pathway is involved in numerous cancers. Monitoring its overactivation by PET imaging remains challenging, yet it holds significant potential for personalized diagnostics. Here, we report the fluorine-18 isotopic radiolabeling of binimetinib, an FDA-approved specific allosteric MEK1/2 inhibitor, for the treatment of BRAF-positive melanoma. The inherent structure of binimetinib makes its radiolabeling a strong challenge, addressed by evaluating seven precursors using a simplified model compound. A fully automated, four-step, one-pot radiosynthesis afforded [18F]binimetinib with a 9 ± 5% radiochemical yield after 100 min with >95% radiochemical purity. In vitro evaluation of [18F]binimetinib demonstrated specific uptake in H358 cells with activated Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK. PET imaging of an H358 xenograft mouse model revealed promising tumor uptake at 4 h post-injection with 1.96 ± 0.51 % ID.cm−3 in the tumor. This study provides insight into the in vivo pharmacokinetic profile derived from PET imaging of [18F]binimetinib and its potential for investigating MEK target availability in tumors.

item.title: Development of Second Generation Thieno[2,3- d ]pyrimidin-4-one Derivatives as Positive Allosteric Modulators of the N -Methyl- d -Aspartate Receptor
item.description:
Abstract
The N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) is a ligated-gated cation channel that mediates excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. These receptors are involved in important brain functions and have been implicated in many neuropathological conditions. Four GluN2 subunits assemble with GluN1 to produce a series of NMDAR subtypes that are expressed in different subpopulations of neurons at different times. Among the GluN2 subunits, the GluN2D-containing NMDARs are highly expressed in inhibitory interneurons, which are key targets for drug development. Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) have been proposed to be useful in several neuropsychiatric indications, including schizophrenia and depression. We have previously discovered EU 1622-240, a novel GluN2B/C/D-biased PAM with favorable oral bioavailability, CNS exposure, and anxiolytic activity in rodents. However, it was a P-gp inhibitor, cleared rapidly, and poorly absorbed in vivo. Through an extensive SAR, we now present EU 1622-287 with improved solubility, oral bioavailability, brain exposure, and anxiolytic effects.

item.title: Discovery of an RNF126-Dependent Polθ Degrader Exhibiting In Vivo Activity in an HR-Deficient Tumor Model
item.description:
Abstract
DNA polymerase theta (Polθ), a multidomain DNA repair enzyme, has emerged as a promising synthetic-lethal target in homologous recombination (HR)-deficient tumors, yet current inhibitors directed at either its helicase or polymerase domain may not fully suppress the functions of the intact protein. Here, we report PR-6, a RNF126-dependent Polθ degrader identified through comparative degrader screening and structural optimization. In BRCA1-deficient MDA-MB-436 cells, PR-6 induced, concentration- and time-dependent Polθ degradation via an RNF126- and ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent mechanism. Compared with the Polθ helicase inhibitor AB25583 under the tested cellular conditions, PR-6 exhibited greater antiproliferative activity and induced more pronounced DNA damage and apoptosis. Moreover, PR-6 synergized with Olaparib in vitro and markedly potentiated its antitumor efficacy in an MDA-MB-436 xenograft model without overt toxicity. These findings support PR-6 as the first degrader probe for interrogating Polθ biology and provide proof of concept for Polθ degradation as a complementary strategy in HR-deficient tumors.

item.title: Scaffold Hopping from Quinazoline to Tetrahydropyrido[3,4- d ]pyrimidine: Enhancing the Potency and Selectivity of HIV-1 Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
In this work, a series of tetrahydropyrido[3,4-d]pyrimidine derivatives were rationally designed as HIV-1 non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors via scaffold modification. Most compounds demonstrated promising potency against wild-type HIV-1 (IIIB) and clinically relevant mutants. Notably, 10p showed the strongest activity against HIV-1 IIIB, L100I, K103N, Y188C, Y188L, and E138K (EC50 = 2.4−16.5 nM). Importantly, 10p maintained potent efficacy against F227L/V106A (EC50 = 12.3 nM) and K103N/Y181C (EC50 = 21.7 nM). In vitro assessment revealed that the metabolic clearance rate of 10p in human liver microsomes was moderately lower than that of rilpivirine. Additionally, 10p showed a low potential for CYP-mediated drug interactions and had a negligible inhibitory effect on the hERG potassium channel. In the acute oral toxicity study in mice, no adverse effects were observed at a dose of up to 2000 mg/kg. These findings identify 10p as a promising lead compound for further development.

item.title: Toward Distributed Robustness in Resistance-Aware Lead Optimization
item.description:
Abstract
Drug resistance often enters lead optimization after a compound has been chosen. We define distributed robustness as redistributing predicted binding support away from predefined mutable contacts while retaining wild-type feasibility and panel coverage. ResistAgent separates site-level and observed combination-level liabilities, diagnoses their structural effects, and compares a matched-budget robust objective with an average-affinity comparator. Across 10 EGFR pairs, the median reduction in hotspot dependence, ΔDep (naive − robust; positive values favor the robust objective), was +0.042; across 9 valid HIV-RT pairs, it was +0.026. Panel passing was preserved but not improved: both objectives passed in every valid pair. ABL1 yielded 2/4 pairs without a corresponding robustness gain. The objective changes the dependence organization and candidate selection. Provider comparisons, ranking benchmarks, and explicit-water contact descriptors are reported alongside the primary endpoint.

item.title: What Does Generalizable AI in Drug Discovery Really Mean?
item.description:
Abstract
Machine learning models increasingly contribute to drug discovery, but their utility depends on performing reliably in their intended deployment setting. Although model generalization is invoked frequently, the drug discovery community lacks a shared vocabulary for how models actually achieve transferability beyond their training data. We argue that achieving generalization requires examining how a model’s inductive bias interacts with its training data to shape the notion of similarity it learns. Without a bias that makes relevant recurring relationships easier to learn as opposed to incidental correlations, models exploit dataset-specific shortcuts. These shortcuts yield high benchmark performance but fail in prospective applications. We therefore propose evaluation principles tailored to a model’s architecture, using diagnostic controls and train−test splits that distinguish transferable learning from the retrieval of familiar training data. This Perspective shows how representational choices shape failure modes across pose-dependent, pose-independent, and foundation model paradigms, and provides a practical framework to help researchers expose shortcuts and interpret predictions.

item.title: ATTEC-Based Autophagic Elimination of HBV Core Protein Achieves Potent Viral Suppression
item.description:
Abstract
HBV core protein (HBc) plays key roles in the viral lifecycle and hepatocarcinogenesis. While core protein allosteric modulators (CpAMs) have emerged as promising therapeutic agents, they are confronted with the issue of emerging drug resistance and lack the ability to degrade HBc. To surmount these challenges, by leveraging the class II CpAM NVR3-778 and an LC3 ligand ispinesib, we identified TK-96, a first-in-class autophagy-tethering compound (ATTEC) degrader, which induces the degradation of wild-type and drug-resistant HBc via the autophagic-lysosomal pathway. Remarkably, TK-96 exhibited subnanomolar antiviral potency in HepAD38 and HBV-infected HLCZ01 cells, indicating a more than 150-fold improvement in potency compared to NVR3-778. Furthermore, oral administration of TK-96 significantly inhibited viral replication and decreased hepatic HBc, as well as serum HBeAg and HBsAg levels, in an HBV carrier mouse model. Collectively, this study identifies a highly potent HBc degrader and underscores ATTEC-mediated degradation as a novel strategy for anti-HBV therapeutics.

item.title: Novel Spiroisatin Derivatives Potentially Useful for Preventing Myocardial Reperfusion Injury
item.description:
Abstract
Ischemia−reperfusion injury remains a major clinical challenge due to mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death. Here we report a novel series of spiroisatin derivatives as modulators of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) targeted at the c-ring of F1/FO-ATP synthase. Structure−activity relationship analysis identified compound 15j with nanomolar in vitro potency in inhibiting mPTP opening while preserving ATP production. Molecular modeling supported distinct binding interactions within the c subunit of F1/FO-ATP synthase, rationalizing observed pharmacodynamics. Beyond mPTP inhibition, 15j positively modulates mitochondrial quality control pathways, including mitophagy and biogenesis, contributing to sustained mitochondrial homeostasis after reperfusion. These findings establish spiroisatin derivatives as a promising class of cardioprotective agents acting through convergent mechanisms on mitochondrial integrity and quality control.

item.title: Ubiquitination-Informed Reinforcement Learning Linker Generator Enables Discovery of Novel FGFR4 PROTAC Degraders
item.description:
Abstract
Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) represent a promising therapeutic strategy, yet rational linker design is limited by inadequate theoretical guidance. Herein, we report PotentialLinker, a novel reinforcement learning framework for PROTAC linker optimization that uses a normalized weighted harmonic mean (NWHM) score to predict degradation activity. Benchmarking on ternary structures confirms its performance without precomputed protein−protein complexes. In case studies of STAT3/RIPK1, it recapitulated structure−activity relationships (SAR) and recommended appropriate E3 ligases. Then, conducted by PotentialLinker, a potent FGFR4 degrader D11 was obtained (DC50 = 56.23 nM, Dmax = 89.58%). Due to its covalent interacting with the unique Cys552 in FGFR4, D11 possesses excellent FGFR4 selectivity. Furthermore, D11 also demonstrated favorable oral bioavailability (F = 21.3%) and potent antitumor efficacy (TGI = 87.07%) with acceptable tolerability in vivo. Taken together, this framework effectively bridges degradation theory and practical PROTAC design, which can be utilized for the rational design of PROTAC-based therapeutic agents.

item.title: Defining the Diphyllin Pharmacophore for Broad-Spectrum Antiviral V-ATPase Inhibition by Structure-Guided Scaffold Modifications
item.description:
Abstract
The threat of emerging viral diseases presents a critical societal need for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics. A key contribution to antiviral options would be a broad-spectrum agent that can treat a wide variety of viral diseases. Vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase), a host proton pump critical for endosomal acidification, serves an essential role in facilitating the entry of multiple viruses. Diphyllin, a naturally occurring V-ATPase inhibitor, displays potent antiviral activity but is limited by suboptimal drug-like properties, including selectivity and metabolic instability. Molecular modeling enabled the identification of a conserved binding site on the V-ATPase a-subunit consisting of three distinct sub-pockets. Docking analyses of ninety-five known diphyllin derivatives demonstrated that active analogs effectively occupy all three subpockets, informing a structure-based design approach. A library of novel diphyllin analogs with modifications to a single-ring system showed 50-fold increases in potency for antiviral activity against Ebola, Venezuelan equine encephalitis, and Chikungunya viruses and exhibiting improvements in metabolic stability and permeability.

item.title: Engineering Camptothecin Prodrugs for Cancer Therapy: An Exposure-First Perspective
item.description:
Abstract
Camptothecin (CPT)-derived anticancer agents stabilize topoisomerase I (TOP1)−DNA cleavage complexes (TOP1ccs), but their therapeutic utility is constrained by lactone instability, variable pharmacokinetics, and systemic toxicity. This Perspective evaluates prodrug strategies according to their initiating activation mechanisms, distinguishing self-immolative chemistry as a payload-release module. Small-molecule prodrugs are emphasized, alongside peptide−drug conjugates, antibody−drug conjugates, polymeric prodrugs, and nanoprodrugs. We propose an exposure-first, “design backward, validate forward” framework in which intended tumor exposure to active lactone and TOP1cc formation guide the payload selection, attachment site, activation compartment, linker kinetics, and delivery platform. Translational evaluation should establish colocalization of intact prodrug and accessible activating stimulus, faithful release of the intended payload, and a favorable balance between tumor exposure and exposure in dose-limiting normal tissues. Additional platform complexity should yield measurable pharmacological benefits. This framework provides practical criteria for prioritizing CPT prodrugs with the potential to improve the therapeutic index.

item.title: A Novel Mathematical Model for Predicting the Agonist Activity of Mixtures Containing Agonist and Antagonist Ligands in Drug Discovery Screening
item.description:
Abstract
Mixture-based positional scanning libraries have been used to identify novel ligands for a variety of targets, including G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). These mixtures may contain both agonist and antagonist ligands. Herein, a mathematical model is derived and experimentally verified to explore the effects of agonist screening in the presence of antagonists and address the decades-old question, “How can you find agonists in the presence of antagonists in mixtures?” This model is used to predict the behavior of agonist-antagonist mixtures at the melanocortin-3 and -4 (MC3R and MC4R) receptors. Based upon this model and these data, it is concluded that only in cases with a large percentage of high-potency antagonists is the agonist signal suppressed below detection levels, explaining why the presence of both ligand classes has not masked potent agonist compounds in mixture-based screening campaigns. The approaches herein may be applied globally to other robust, reproducible assays testing mixtures.

item.title: Discovery and Preclinical Characterization of Benzofuran Derivatives as Potent, Selective, and Orally Bioavailable GSPT1 Molecular Glue Degraders for the Treatment of MYC-Driven Cancers
item.description:
Abstract
Targeted protein degradation of the translation termination factor GSPT1 is a promising cancer strategy. However, current cereblon-recruiting molecular glue degraders (MGDs) lack structural diversity, being mostly IMiD derivatives. To overcome resistance and improve drug-like properties, we report the rational, structure-guided design of a novel series of benzofuran-based GSPT1 MGDs. Extensive structure−activity relationship studies and optimization led to the discovery of highly potent, orally bioavailable degraders, highlighted by compounds C-3 and C-4. Both exhibited single-digit nanomolar GSPT1 degradation (DC50 = 2.81 and 1.91 nM) and robust selectivity over IMiD off-targets IKZF1 and SALL4. In vivo, oral administration (1−2 mg/kg) of C-3 and C-4 demonstrated favorable cross-species pharmacokinetics and achieved sustained tumor regression in NCI-H1155 and MDA-MB-468 xenograft models. With a maximum tolerated dose exceeding 100 mg/kg and no hematological toxicity, these benzofuran-based MGDs are highly promising preclinical candidates for solid tumors.

item.title: Photoactivatable Small-Molecule PD-L1 Inhibitors for Checkpoint Blockade-based Tumor Immunotherapy
item.description:
Abstract
Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction shows remarkable antitumor efficacy clinically but systemic administration can cause immune-related adverse events in multiple organs from nonspecific T-cell activation, restricting the clinical safety window. Achieving spatiotemporal regulation of immune checkpoint blockadepreserving antitumor immunity while avoiding systemic toxicityis a key challenge. Prodrug strategies, particularly photocaging, enable on-demand light-triggered drug activation. Here, we propose a prodrug design for small-molecule PD-L1 inhibitors using coumarin photocaging groups. Guided by cocrystal binding mode analysis, we covalently masked two inhibitors with coumarin photolabile protecting groups, and designed and synthesized the corresponding photocaged prodrugs. In vitro, the prodrugs were inactive under dark conditions, but upon visible light activation, they restored T-cell effector function and restored T-cell effector function in PD-L1-dependent co-culture models. These results validate the on-demand release pharmacological property, providing a feasible approach for spatiotemporally controllable immunotherapy in superficial or optically accessible lesions.

item.title: Photoswitchable Inhibitors Targeting the Glucose Transporter GLUT1
item.description:
Abstract
Based on azologization and structural simplification of the potent glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) inhibitor BAY-876, nine novel azo compounds were designed, synthesized and evaluated towards their applicability as photoswitchable GLUT1 inhibitors. Eight candidates showed suitable photochemical properties, whereat the compounds reached a photostationary state (PSS365) between 96% cis and 87% cis while being largely present as trans isomers (between 99% and 76%) under ambient light. Moreover, the azo compounds did not give any hint of decomposition after multiple forth-and-back switching events. Biological investigations using recombinant and cancer-derived cell models demonstrated that the three cis isomers of PWH203 (1), PWH448 (2) and LLH003 (6) show remarkable GLUT1 inhibition while the corresponding trans isomers are more or less inactive. These results lay the groundwork towards improved targeting in cancer therapy, where GLUT1 inhibitors are only active in the irradiated target tissue while converting back to their inactive state when leaving this area.

item.title: A Dual SIRT6/Classical HDAC Inhibitor with Integrated Antiproliferative, Antimigratory, and Pharmacokinetic Advantages Against Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Pancreatic cancer (PC) is highly malignant, with a poor prognosis and high metastatic potential. Given the synergy between sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) and classical histone deacetylase (HDAC) in regulating epithelial−mesenchymal transition (EMT), dual-target inhibitors may offer improved antimetastatic therapy. The lead compound 11e suffers from poor metabolic stability, weak antiproliferative activity, and insufficient antimigratory capacity. Through pharmacophore merging and structural optimization, we obtained S20, which potently inhibits SIRT6 (IC50 = 3.903 μM) and classical HDACs (IC50 = 0.217 μM). In vitro, S20 was superior to 11e in antiproliferative activity and showed stronger antimigratory activity than SAHA, 11e, or their combination. Mechanistically, S20 modulated EMT-associated marker expression, increasing E-cadherin while decreasing N-cadherin, vimentin, and ZEB1. Its intravenous half-life (4.11 h) was 14.7-fold longer than 11e (0.28 h). In vivo, S20 dose-dependently suppressed liver metastasis with favorable safety. In summary, S20 exhibits comprehensive advantages in antiproliferative, antimigratory, and metabolic stability, providing a new strategy for antimetastatic drug development.

item.title: Combinatorial Synthesis and Direct-to-Biology Antibacterial Evaluation of Ruthenium(II) and Iridium(III) N^O -Schiff−Base Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a major global health challenge, compounded by a limited antibiotic discovery pipeline and restricted chemical diversity among clinically used antibiotics. Metal-based complexes offer promising antimicrobial agents owing to their structural diversity and unique modes of action. Here, we report the synthesis and biological evaluation of two combinatorial libraries comprising 176 novel ruthenium(II) p-cymene (RuCy) and iridium(III) Cp* (IrCp) N^O-Schiff-base complexes. Syntheses used a robust three-step, room-temperature methodology, with automated LC−MS characterization enabling Direct-to-Biology screening. Against Staphylococcus aureus, 50−80% of compounds inhibited growth, whereas no significant activity was observed against Escherichia coli. Three leads exhibited MICs of 1.56−12.5 μM against Gram-positive pathogens, therapeutic indices exceeding 15, and negligible haemolysis. Mechanistic studies suggest that IrCp-B5, incorporating the ligand (E)-2-bromo-4-chloro-6-(((naphthalen-2-ylmethyl)imino)methyl)phenol, disrupts membrane associated processes, while RuCy-J3, incorporating (E)-1-((cyclohexylimino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol, targets intracellular DNA-related pathways. This work demonstrates the utility of Direct-to-Biology approaches for accelerated antimicrobial lead identification and prioritization.

item.title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of 68 Ga-Labeled BCMA-Targeting Nanobodies for PET Imaging of Multiple Myeloma
item.description:
Abstract
B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a critical biomarker for multiple myeloma (MM). In this study, three 68Ga-labeled BCMA-targeting nanobodies (C02, C06, and C07) were developed and evaluated. Protein-based binding assays showed apparent nanomolar affinities, with dissociation constants of 58 ± 7 nM, 87 ± 9 nM, and 33 ± 3 nM, respectively. Their BCMA specificities were confirmed by the high BCMA-positive H929 cell uptakes (6.08 ± 0.73%, 4.59 ± 0.45%, and 4.05 ± 0.29% at 0.5 h, respectively) and significant inhibition (82%, 88%, and 66%, respectively) by the unlabeled nanobodies. [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-BCMA-C07 exhibited the most favorable profile in microPET/CT imaging, with tumor uptake of 3.26 ± 0.19% ID/g, renal uptake of 13.61 ± 1.90% ID/g, and tumor-to-muscle ratio of 7.46 ± 2.82 at 0.5 h post-injection (p.i.). These findings support [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-BCMA-C07 as a promising BCMA-targeted PET radiotracer with potential for further clinical translation.

item.title: Design, Synthesis and Evaluation of QuAOCOM-Linked Halogenated Phenazines as Potent Antibacterial and Biofilm-Killing Agents
item.description:
Abstract
Bacterial biofilms are surface-attached communities with enriched populations of non-replicating persister cells. As such, biofilms are credited as the underlying cause of chronic and recurring bacterial infections. Unlike free-floating, replicating planktonic bacteria that can acquire resistance to conventional antibiotic treatments, metabolically-dormant biofilm communities exhibit intrinsic tolerance to all classes of antibiotics. To address challenges associated with bacterial biofilms, our lab has identified halogenated phenazine (HP) small molecules that demonstrate outstanding antibacterial and biofilm-killing activities via iron starvation. Here, we report the design, chemical synthesis, and evaluation of a focused series of quinone alkyloxycarbonyloxymethyl(QuAOCOM)-linked HP prodrugs. During these studies, we found QuAOCOM-linked HPs 22 and 27 to demonstrate very good linker stability, rapid processing of the quinone trigger, improved water solubilities, potent antibacterial and biofilm eradication activities, and favorable cytotoxicity profiles. These studies highlight important features related to the design of HP prodrug conjugates which could have a significant impact addressing problems associated with antibiotic-tolerant biofilms.

item.title: A Portable N-Terminal Biphenyl Motif in LL-37 Enhances the Activity of Short Human Cathelicidin Derivatives
item.description:
Abstract
Issues such as potency and stability limit our ability to realize the potential of host defense peptides to serve as new antibiotics. Informed by our prior structure−activity work, we demonstrate that transposition of an N-terminal biphenyl motif from full-length LL-37 onto the previously-described central activity region (residues 18−29) improves activity against Gram-negative bacteria by >16-fold. We further improve upon this lead derivative, termed FF-14, using stabilizing modifications such as d-amino acids and C-terminal amidation as well as selected N-lipidation moieties and demonstrate the transferability of biphenyl motif activity to longer cathelicidin scaffolds. Mechanistic interrogation reveals that the biphenyl pharmacophore increases both inner and outer membrane permeabilization while promoting a helical structure in the 14-mer without directly impacting peptide stability. Inclusion of the LL-37 biphenyl motif is thus a portable strategy for augmenting short cathelicidin activity and better approximating the activity profile of LL-37 itself in short sequences.

item.title: Identification of Novel RORγt Inverse Agonist YW-089 as a Preclinical Candidate for the Treatment of Autoimmune Diseases
item.description:
Abstract
Retinoic acid receptor-related orphan receptor γt (RORγt) is a key regulator of IL-17-producing T helper 17 (Th17) cell differentiation and an attractive target for autoimmune diseases. Although RORγt inverse agonists have shown clinical promise, identifying candidates with both high potency and favorable drug-like properties remain challenging. We previously reported the carboxyl-containing biaryl urea compound 3i, which reduced psoriasis severity in mice but exhibited poor microsomal stability and suboptimal pharmacokinetics (38% oral bioavailability in mice). Herein, optimization of sulfone-containing biaryl ureas led to the discovery of compound 4 (YW-089), a potent and selective RORγt inverse agonist (RORγ FRET IC50 = 27 nM; mTh17 IC50 = 140 nM). YW-089 demonstrated markedly improved metabolic stability across species (t1/2 > 145 min), favorable pharmacokinetics in mice, rats, and dogs (oral bioavailability 66%, 65%, and 73%, respectively), and robust efficacy in imiquimod- and IL-23-induced psoriasis mouse models, supporting its further preclinical development for autoimmune diseases.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of 99m Tc-Labeled PSMA-Targeting Dimeric Tracers: Comparison of Glutamate−Urea−Lysine (EuK) and Aminoadipic Acid−Urea−Lysine (AuK) Targeting Groups
item.description:
Abstract
In clinical practice of prostate cancer (PCa) management, the high renal uptake of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiotracers remains a significant concern. To address this challenge, the study systematically evaluated molecular modification strategiestargeting moieties, linker types, and coligand compositionsfor their effects on tracer pharmacokinetics. Among candidates, [99mTc]Tc-EuK2-LPRO-HYNIC-EDDA was the most promising for single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging. It binds PSMA stably with nanomolar affinity (Kd = 16.28 nM), and the high blocking efficiency in vitro and in vivo subsequently confirmed excellent targeting specificity. The tracer cleared rapidly from nontarget organs, effectively mitigating renal accumulation and giving high target-to-background ratios. Crucially, high-contrast SPECT/CT images obtained 2−6 h post-injection indicate clinical promise for routine and delayed PCa imaging. Additionally, density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provided critical theoretical insights into coordination structure, ligand−protein interaction mechanisms, and correlations between conformational differences and biological activity.

item.title: Why Breakthrough Drug Discovery Platforms Need Decades to Mature: Lessons from FBDD, DEL, Aptamers, and PROTACs
item.description:
Abstract
Breakthrough hit-finding platforms rarely become routine after the first novel proof-of-concept and realistically take 20−30 years to develop fully. Across FBDD, DEL, Aptamer, and PROTAC drug discovery technologies, the persistent rate-limiting issue in platform development is not the founding concept alone (e.g., chemistry) rather, it is often more likely due to organizations underestimating the time to develop a robust technique in-house and the significant supporting infrastructure and talent required to transform novel technologies into routine hit-finding drug discovery platforms. A consequence for not being “all in” on its development can be a dilution of effort across programs that may lead to fewer clinical candidates and a decrease in ROI. As a result, it can take decades not years to develop a platform. Using lessons learned from these four platforms, this Perspective identifies key (and often unappreciated) hurdles that each new technology needs to resolve before becoming a mainstream hit-finding drug discovery platform driving FDA approvals.

item.title: Design and Synthesis of Novel Mitochondria-Targeted HDAC3 Inhibitors for the Treatment of Obesity
item.description:
Abstract
Obesity is closely associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, which impairs fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism, yet currently available HDAC3 inhibitors have not been optimized to address these metabolic abnormalities. Herein, we developed a series of mitochondria-targeted HDAC3 inhibitors by incorporating a TPP moiety into the classical HDAC pharmacophore. Structure-based optimization identified H18 (IC50 = 45.4 nM) as the most promising candidate, exhibiting potent HDAC3 inhibitory activity together with preferential mitochondrial localization. H18 effectively suppressed lipid accumulation during 3T3-L1 adipocyte differentiation while restoring intracellular ATP levels and reducing oxidative stress. In diet-induced obese mice, H18 produced dose-dependent reductions in body weight gain, improved glucose tolerance, and insulin sensitivity and exhibited superior efficacy to BG45. Collectively, these findings identify H18 as a promising antiobesity lead compound and support the integration of mitochondrial targeting capability into HDAC3 inhibitor design as a promising strategy for obesity intervention.

item.title: Design of High-Affinity Mini-Protein Drug Conjugates Targeting TROP2
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate and effective treatment of solid tumors has long been a core issue in cancer therapy. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent a crucial breakthrough in precision oncology. Traditional ADCs rely on monoclonal antibodies generated through animal immunization, followed by screening, sequencing, and recombinant expressiona process that is experimentally complex and costly. In this study, we employed deep learning-based computational design methods to design mini-protein binders targeting the tumor-associated antigen TROP2. The designed TROP2 mini-protein binder exhibited high specificity and thermal stability. The binding affinity was optimized from 40.4 nM to 628 pM through partial diffusion. On this basis, we engineered the mini-protein binder by conjugating it with the microtubule inhibitor VcMMAE, thereby constructing mini-protein drug conjugates (MPDCs) that can specifically target and kill TROP2-positive tumor cells. A comprehensive assessment of the anti-tumor efficacy of these MPDCs was performed using cancer cell lines, organoid models, and mouse xenograft models.

item.title: The Human ADME Score: Quantifying the ADME Performance of Oral Therapeutics
item.description:
Abstract
Quantifying ADME-related drug-likeness is challenging as drug discovery expands into larger, more complex molecules. We developed the human ADME Score to assess oral drug-likeness through functional ADME properties, positioned between molecular descriptors and clinical pharmacokinetic outcomes. The continuous score (0−1) integrates experimental or machine-learning-predicted solubility, passive permeability, free hepatocyte intrinsic clearance, P-gp efflux, and plasma fraction unbound using Softmin-5, balancing minimum and average values. Datasets of 32,307 nonclinical and 588 clinical compounds with over 123 thousand ADME measurements were used for the construction and evaluation. Scores were higher in clinical than nonclinical compounds and varied across projects, target classes, and chemotypes. The score achieved the highest observed correlation and discrimination among evaluated comparators, supporting compound comparison and prioritization. Endpoint scores highlight potential ADME liabilities. Current application is best supported for molecules ≤1000 Da, reflecting chemical representation and assay validity.

item.title: Narrow-Spectrum Oxadiazole Antibacterials that Target Cell−Wall Septation in Clostridioides difficile and Spare the Gut Microbiota
item.description:
Abstract
Recurrence of infection is a challenge in treatment of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), observed in 25% of patients. The first-line antibiotics disturb the gut microbiota, exacerbating the already disrupted commensal gut homeostasis and allow for C. difficile colonization. Narrow-spectrum antibiotics are critical for selective targeting of C. difficile while preserving beneficial gut flora, thereby mitigating recurrence. Our study investigates a novel class of highly selective, nitroimidazole-based oxadiazole antibacterials. We detail the chemical basis for their exceptional selectivity against C. difficile over commensal bacteria and elucidate their mechanism of action. Oxadiazole 2 inhibits penicillin-binding proteins 1 and 3 involved in septal peptidoglycan biosynthesis during vegetative cell division. We further demonstrate by whole-genome sequencing that treatment of mice with oxadiazole 2 does not disrupt the gut microflora and confers an impediment to colonization by C. difficile. This work is foundational for development of a new generation of narrow-spectrum therapeutics to combat CDI.

item.title: Generative AI-Driven Interpolation of Cross-Family Kinase Space: Discovery of Dual-Targeting Degraders of IRAK4 and TYK2
item.description:
Abstract
Bridging structural discontinuities between disparate protein families is a fundamental challenge in multi-target design. We present a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform for the non-linear interpolation of cross-family kinase space to simultaneously modulate innate (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4, IRAK4) and adaptive (tyrosine kinase 2, TYK2) immunity. Utilizing a variational autoencoder−recurrent neural network (VAE−RNN) model within the POLYGON framework, we successfully navigated high-dimensional latent space through an iterative “sampling−scoring−refocusing” strategy. This approach bypassed the geometric limitations of traditional pharmacophore merging, leading to the rational discovery of a novel spirocyclic scaffold with significant structural novelty (Tanimoto similarity <0.45). Integration of WaterMap-based optimization and proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) conjugation yielded C-8-014, a potent dual-target degrader achieving nanomolar potency and efficient degradation of both kinases. This study demonstrates a validated closed-loop methodology for navigating “unreachable” regions of the kinome, providing a paradigm-shifting approach for cross-family chemical design and a powerful molecular tool for chemical biology.

item.title: [Graphical abstract added] Highlight on Pronidesivir (GS-441524): The First Approved Drug for the Treatment of Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP)
Unbiased, Target-Agnostic Platform for the Synthesis and Screening of PROTAC Libraries
item.description:
Abstract
Most approaches to PROTAC discovery require prior knowledge of the protein target, limiting the scope of targetable biology. Here we report an unbiased, direct-to-biology platform for the high-throughput synthesis and phenotypic screening of PROTAC libraries. The platform employs the Ugi multicomponent reaction to couple diverse carboxylic acid-containing ligands with VHL-recruiting E3 ligase ligand−linker conjugates in a single well plate step, followed by solid-phase extraction and cell-based phenotypic screening without predetermined target selection. A pilot library derived from seven structurally diverse protein ligands was screened in a cell viability assay against six cancer cell lines, yielding potent and selective hits. Global proteomics identified BRD4 as the primary target of lead compound B5, a BI2536-derived VHL-recruiting degrader that exhibited single-digit nanomolar degradation potency (DC50 = 4.9 nM, Dmax = 96%) and complete selectivity for BRD4 over PLK1. Target engagement and ternary complex formation were confirmed by NanoBRET, Western blot, and Boltz-2 computational modeling. The modularity of the Ugi reaction further enabled direct synthesis of two photoaffinity labeling probes, PALTAC-1 and PALTAC-2, which confirmed BRD4 as a direct binding target via photocrosslinking and pull-down experiments. This platform enables the unbiased discovery of degrader drugs and their targets from phenotypic screens and provides a generalizable framework for converting existing compound libraries into functional PROTAC collections.

item.title: Glycosylation Shapes Isoform-Selective Recognition of Flavonoids by Human Glucose Transporters
item.description:
Abstract
Human glucose transporters (GLUTs) are pharmacologically relevant membrane proteins interacting with diverse flavonoids, yet previous studies focused largely on individual isoforms and limited ligand sets. Here, we docked 207 flavonoids against all 14 human GLUT isoforms, complemented by microscale thermophoresis (MST) and membrane-embedded molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Docking revealed heterogeneous interaction profiles associated with differential glycosyl accommodation, distinguishing broad glycosylated flavonoid−preferring (gly-flav−preferring; e.g., GLUT1) and aglycone-biased (agly-flav−biased; e.g., GLUT3) groups. Glycosyl size generally outweighed attachment position, with gly-flav−preferring GLUTs tending to favor larger glycosides and agly-flav−biased GLUTs showing weaker or less favorable responses to glycosyl enlargement. Consistently, MST revealed enhanced GLUT1 binding for selected diglycosides relative to monoglycosides. MD further showed more favorable calculated binding energies for GLUT1 than GLUT3, with size predominating in GLUT1 and position contributing more prominently in GLUT3. Together, these findings highlight glycosylation as a context-dependent determinant of GLUT−flavonoid recognition.

item.title: Autonomous Drug Design via Workflow Agents: Integrating Chemical Semantics and Tool-Oriented Automation
item.description:
Abstract
Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown promise in automating scientific tasks, yet existing systems for drug discovery often lack strategic, cross-step planning, and multi-objective coordination. Here, we present drugflow-skills, an LLM-driven agent framework that abstracts key drug design operations, including virtual screening, de novo molecule generation, molecular optimization, and multi-target design, into composable and reusable skills. The agent operates under a ReAct paradigm, executing iterative “Thought → Action → Observation” loops while interfacing with the DrugFlow backend. Across five representative tasks targeting ALK, ROS1, and IGF-1R, the agent demonstrates autonomous decision-making, cross-step planning, and multi-objective trade-offs, achieving improved predicted binding scores while reducing predicted toxicity and off-target liabilities. It also provides interpretable rationales and adapts strategies based on human feedback, enabling a human-agent co-optimization loop. These results support dynamic reasoning-driven drug design.

item.title: Broad-Spectrum Antimicrobial Peptide Designed from the Mycobacterium tuberculosis Adenylate Kinase Structure, Inspired by Its LPS/LTA Dual Recognition
item.description:
Abstract
Broad-spectrum therapeutics targeting multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens remain limited. Utilizing structural insights from Mycobacterium tuberculosis adenylate kinase (MtAdk), which uniquely recognizes both lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and lipoteichoic acid (LTA), we designed broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptides. Through incorporation of non-natural amino acids, terminal acylation, and arginine extension, we developed a lead candidate, YK-mAK-17, with remarkable stability, minimal resistance development, and broad-spectrum activity, particularly against carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Mechanistic studies revealed an amphipathic α-helix with N-terminal C6 acylation that enhances membrane engagement, driving rapid bactericidal activity via multimodal disruption of membrane integrity and virulence pathways. In septic shock mouse models induced by CRAB and MRSA, YK-mAK-17 significantly improved survival and reduced organ damage. By combining MtAdk-inspired dual LPS/LTA recognition with targeted chemical modifications, YK-mAK-17 represents a promising antimicrobial candidate possessing broad-spectrum antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties, highlighting the potential of structure-guided peptide design for addressing MDR infections.

item.title: Lipid-Modified CGRP Receptor Antagonists: Balancing Pharmacokinetic Improvement and Potency Loss
item.description:
Abstract
Lipidation is a promising strategy for enhancing peptide stability by reducing proteolytic degradation and prolonging systemic exposure. In this study, we systematically evaluated lipid motifs varying in lipid chain length and PEG spacer composition, combined with peptide N-terminal modifications, using a 10-mer calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist to optimize a candidate for migraine treatment. Incorporation of a C18 diacid lipid motif increased the in vivo (mouse) half-life to 3.5 h. Although lipidation improved serum stability in a size-dependent manner, it was accompanied by a reduction in receptor antagonism, highlighting the balance between pharmacokinetic enhancement and biological activity. These findings improve our understanding of the trade-offs involved in lipidated peptide design and support future optimization strategies. In addition, we developed a rapid, inexpensive, and HPLC-compatible assay for quantifying peptide binding to human serum albumin, overcoming limitations of conventional equilibrium dialysis methods, including non-specific membrane binding, lengthy equilibration times, and peptide degradation.

item.title: Discovery of F73, a New Generation RET Inhibitor Overcoming RET Gatekeeper (V804M) and Solvent-Front (G810C/R) Mutations
item.description:
Abstract
Pharmacological invention of RET offers a compelling strategy to treat patients harboring RET fusions or mutations. Selective RET inhibitors, including pralsetinib and selpercatinib, have demonstrated substantial clinical benefits. However, this efficacy is often compromised by the occurrence of resistance, particularly RET solvent front mutations G810C/R. To address this problem, we performed a systematic structure−activity optimization based on our reported RET inhibitors. Our efforts yielded F73, a next generation RET inhibitor with potent activity against RET mutations including V804M and G810C/R. F73 effectively suppressed RET phosphorylation and downstream SHC activation in Ba/Fa3 cells harboring various RET resistance mutations. Furthermore, it induced apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest in a dose-dependent manner in CCDC6-RET and CCDC6-RET-G810R Ba/F3 cells. Notably, F73 exhibited robust antitumor efficacy in Ba/F3-RET-G810R xenograft models, outperforming selpercatinib, thus supporting its potential to overcome resistance mediated by RET gatekeeper (V804M) and solvent-front (G810C/R) mutations.

item.title: Potent and Selective Caspase-2 Inhibitors: Biological Profiling, Structural Characterization, and Challenges of Molecular Instability
item.description:
Abstract
Caspase-2 (Casp2) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases due to its role in pathological tau processing. Here, we designed and synthesized a series of 48 novel peptidomimetic Casp2 inhibitors organized into distinct structural classes. Compounds were evaluated for Casp2 inhibition and selectivity against Casp1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10. Inhibitors Idc(hE)G(Dab)D-CHO (32) and Idc(hE)G((S)-Me-THIQ)D-CHO (33) exhibited low nanomolar potency and ≥537-fold selectivity over Casp3. These unprecedented scaffold modifications are consistent with preferred steric arrangements between the P2 and P3 positions. Biochemical assays demonstrated the blockade of tau truncation and impaired the formation of toxic Δtau314. High-resolution crystal structures of compounds 2 and 33 bound to Casp2 revealed binding interactions consistent with the observed SAR. Although Idc(hE)V((S)-Me-THIQ)D-CHO (3, MUR-65) showed favorable ADME and pharmacokinetic properties, limited membrane permeability, insufficient blood−brain barrier penetration, and P5 indoline instability remain key challenges for further development.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of a Potent NLRP3 Inflammasome Inhibitor with Favorable Pharmacokinetic and Safety Profiles for Chronic Inflammatory Diseases
item.description:
Abstract
Persistent NLRP3 activation drives chronic inflammatory diseases, necessitating inhibitors with sustained exposure and tolerability. Rational optimization of the hydrophobic and solvent-exposed regions of MCC950 yielded sulfonylurea F34, which inhibited NLRP3-dependent IL-1β release (IC50 = 38.81 nM), with nanomolar potency similar to MCC950, without apparent NLRC4 or AIM2 inhibition. Docking predicted that F34 binds within the MCC950 pocket, where it generally remained during a 200 ns MD simulation. SPR confirmed direct NLRP3 binding (KD = 2.12 μM). In mice, F34 exhibited an oral half-life of 11.89 h and oral bioavailability of 91.36%, potentially contributing to greater efficacy than MCC950 in MSU-induced gouty arthritis and chronic DSS-induced colitis. F34 also showed better tolerability than MCC950 in acute high-dose and 14 day repeated-dose studies, together with weak hERG-channel inhibition (IC50 > 40 μM) and limited CYP inhibition. Thus, optimization preserved nanomolar cellular potency while improving oral exposure, in vivo efficacy, and preliminary tolerability.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Indolin-2-one Derivatives as Novel Covalent Pan-FGFR Inhibitors for Overcoming Clinical Resistance
item.description:
Abstract
Oncogenic FGFR alterations drive the development of multiple cancers. However, acquired resistance to clinically approved inhibitors mediated by gatekeeper and molecular brake mutations poses a major therapeutic challenge. Herein, we describe the structure-based discovery of (Z)-3-(amino(phenyl)methylene)indolin-2-one derivatives as potent covalent pan-FGFR inhibitors. The representative compound, 9v, displayed high potency against FGFR1/2/3/4 (IC50 = 8.6, 5.4, 4.4, and 6.9 nM, respectively) and potent antiproliferative effects across a panel of FGFR-driven cancer cell lines (IC50 = 0.3−6.1 nM). Notably, 9v retained high efficacy against common resistance mutations, including the gatekeeper (FGFR1 V561M, FGFR2 V564F, and FGFR3 V555M) and “molecular brake” (FGFR2 N549K) variants, with IC50 values of <0.1 nM. Covalent modification of FGFR3 by 9v was confirmed through MALDI-TOF-MS and LC−MS/MS-based site mapping. Furthermore, 9v exhibited significant antitumor efficacy in an RT112/84 bladder cancer xenograft model, providing a promising strategy to overcome resistance in FGFR-targeted therapy.

item.title: Enthalpy-Informed Design of Dasatinib-Derived Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Transthyretin Amyloidogenesis
item.description:
Abstract
Transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis is driven by dissociation of the native tetramer into aggregation-prone monomers, making kinetic stabilization of the tetramer an established therapeutic strategy. Here, we demonstrate that binding enthalpy-guided optimization provides an effective strategy for developing selective TTR stabilizers. Starting from a kinase inhibitor-derived scaffold, stepwise optimization comprising scaffold simplification, terminal phenyl modification, and halogen substitution yielded compound 29, which exhibits aggregation inhibitory activity comparable to tafamidis and close to that of acoramidis. Isothermal titration calorimetry revealed that optimization predominantly improved binding enthalpy, while changes in binding free energy were modest. Combined X-ray and neutron crystallographic analyses suggested that the favorable enthalpy originates from enhanced shape complementarity and weak interactions rather than conventional hydrogen bonds. Importantly, compound 29 maintains robust binding to TTR in human plasma. These findings demonstrate that binding enthalpy can serve as a practical parameter for optimizing TTR amyloid inhibitors.

item.title: Small-Molecule Drugs for Glaucoma: IOP-Lowering, Neuroprotective and Multi-Target Strategies
item.description:
Abstract
Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, is primarily driven by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) apoptosis. Small-molecule agents, owing to their high target specificity and excellent ocular tissue penetration, remain the cornerstone of clinical management. This perspective evaluates recent advances in small-molecule glaucoma therapeutics and their pharmacological targets. We first outline the medicinal chemistry, structure−activity relationships (SAR), and clinical status of agents modulating aqueous humor (AH) dynamics, detailing targeted therapies. Given that disease commonly progresses to optic nerve degeneration despite well-controlled IOP, we further summarize developmental trends in neuroprotective molecules designed to directly slow disease progression. We also discuss the rationale, design strategies, clinical translational potential and limitations of dual/multi-target drugs and combination therapies. Collectively, this perspective provides a systematic reference and future outlook for developing next-generation, mechanism-informed therapies for precision glaucoma treatment.

item.title: Diverse Computational Strategies Enable the Discovery of p38α−MK2 Molecular Glues
item.description:
Abstract
Mitogen-activated protein kinase-activated protein kinase 2 (MK2) phosphorylates AU-rich element-binding proteins (AUBPs) that modulate the stability of cytokine mRNA. An emerging class of inhibitors creates a ternary complex between upstream kinase p38α and MK2. These molecular glues demonstrate sustained efficacy relative to orthosteric inhibitors of either p38α or MK2; however, their mechanism of action presents challenges to computationally driven design. Herein we describe in silico hit identification strategies leveraging free energy perturbation coupled with machine learning to triage and prioritize ligands from diverse chemical sources and identify multiple structurally diverse, potent, and highly selective p38α−MK2 molecular glues. Lead compounds 14 and 28 demonstrated an attractive PK profile with sufficient coverage of human whole blood EC50 and displayed pronounced reduction of TNFα levels after PO dosing in lipopolysaccharide mouse models, illustrating the value of our in silico hit identification strategies and optimization of non-degrading molecular glues.

item.title: Synthesis of Amino-Functionalized Abasic Monomers as Versatile Building Blocks for siRNA Modification
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical modification plays a central role in optimizing siRNA therapeutics. Here, we designed and synthesized four amino-functionalized abasic phosphoramidite monomers (Ab1−Ab4) based on tetrahydropyrrole and aminocyclopentane scaffolds. Incorporation of these units destabilized siRNA duplexes in a position-dependent manner, and enhanced silencing activity at central or terminal positions on the sense strand, with the (S)-aminocyclopentane abasic (Ab4) exhibiting the strongest potency. Seed-region incorporation, particularly of the (R)-aminocyclopentane abasic (Ab3), mitigated miRNA-like off-target effects while retaining on-target activity in vitro. Following subcutaneous administration in mice, an Ab4-modified siRNA induced more potent hepatic mRNA knockdown than the parent siRNA at a single dose of 0.1 mg/kg, and Ab3 incorporation significantly reduced the number of off-target transcripts. In addition, 3′-terminal Ab4 incorporation improved nuclease resistance, leading to enhanced hepatic exposure in vivo, and served as a practical linker for conjugation. These findings establish amino-functionalized abasic units as a versatile platform for siRNA modification.

item.title: Highlight on Pronidesivir (GS-441524): The First Approved Drug for the Treatment of Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP)
item.description: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), caused by feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV), is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease, significantly affecting the health and survival of cats, with a mortality rate approaching 100%.1−23 FIP was once considered a fatal disease, and euthanasia was often recommended upon diagnosis due to its extremely poor prognosis.3 FIPV belongs to feline coronavirus (FCoV), an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.4 Based on differences in the spike protein, FCoV is classified into two distinct serotypes, namely, type I and type II.5 Type I FCoV, the predominant serotype worldwide (80−95%), is difficult to culture in vitro. Type I FCoV S protein is entirely derived from FCoV, but the cellular receptor it utilizes remains unidentified.6,7 Type II FCoV is relatively uncommon but easy to culture in vitro, which has made it widely used in laboratory studies.8 Type II FCoV is thought to have arisen from genetic recombination between type I FCoV and canine coronavirus (CCoV), with its S protein gene derived from CCoV.9 Besides serotypes, FCoV is classified by biotype into two forms: feline enteric coronavirus (FECV) and feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV).10 FIPV originates from mutations of FECV, which is widely present in cat populations but generally causes only mild or no clinical signs.10 Additionally, based on clinical presentation, FIP is classified into three forms: the effusive (wet) form, the non-effusive (dry) form, and the mixed form.11−1213 The effusive (wet) form is characterized by massive accumulation of protein-rich fluid in body cavities (e.g., abdominal, thoracic) due to immune-mediated vasculitis.11 The non-effusive (dry) form is characterized by granulomatous lesions in multiple organs,12 while the mixed form presents with features of both.13 The effusive (wet) form is the most classic and readily recognizable manifestation of FIP.11,12

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Preclinical Evaluation of [ 18 F]FPON, a First-In-Class PET Tracer Targeting Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen for Glioblastoma Imaging
item.description:
Abstract
Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is a central regulator of glioma stem cell maintenance and therapy resistance, yet no noninvasive method exists to visualize its expression in vivo. We developed [18F]FPON, a first-in-class small-molecule PET tracer targeting PCNA, derived from the clinical inhibitor AOH1996. FPON binds recombinant PCNA with a Kd of 900.8 ± 131.2 nM, comparable to AOH1996. [18F]FPON is synthesized in one step with a decay-corrected radiochemical yield of 11.43 ± 4.03% (n = 6) and >95% radiochemical purity, readily crosses the blood−brain barrier, and remains >87% intact in brain at 60 min post-injection. In orthotopic U87 glioma xenografts, [18F]FPON exhibits specific tumor uptake (SUVr = 2.58 ± 0.38 vs contralateral brain), which is significantly reduced by AOH1996 (SUVr = 1.62 ± 0.24, p < 0.01). These results establish [18F]FPON as a promising PET tracer for noninvasive imaging of PCNA and support its potential use as a companion diagnostic for PCNA-targeted therapies.

item.title: Exploring Structure−Activity Relationships by Engineering Modified Thrombin Inhibitors from the Flea Xenopsylla cheopis
item.description:
Abstract
Engineering of post-translationally sulfated polypeptides from hematophagous organisms has shown promise for the development of novel anticoagulants with improved therapeutic potential. Here, we describe the development of a high-throughput peptide engineering workflow to facilitate rapid assembly of libraries of modified peptide analogues. Library members were designed from the privileged chimeric anticoagulant sulfo-XC43-Hiru, comprised of a peptide fragment of XC43 (from the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis) and a sulfopeptide fragment of hirudin (from the medicinal leech, Hirudo medicinalis). Focus was placed on exploring the influence of non-native structural motifs through the incorporation of non-canonical amino acids at a number of strategic sites. The thrombin inhibitory activity and cleavage resistance of each analogue is profiled and provides valuable insight into the relationship between the sequence and biological activity of these molecules.

item.title: Precision/Locus-Selective G-Quadruplex Stabilization as the Next Medicinal Chemistry Challenge
item.description:
Abstract
G-quadruplexes (G4s) are druggable nucleic acid structures implicated in gene regulation and disease, but translating G4 ligands into medicines remains difficult because affinity for shared G-tetrad features can produce broad target engagement and obscure locus-specific mechanisms. This Perspective distinguishes topology selectivity from true genomic or transcriptomic selectivity and examines emerging strategies that add sequence addressability or induced proximity to G4 pharmacology. We discuss CRISPR-guided G4 modulation, G4-ligand-oligonucleotide conjugates, and RNA-targeting chimeras, together with earlier sequence-directed polyamide approaches and selective small-molecule precedents. We also consider medicinal chemistry parameters including ligand exit vector, linker architecture, charge, subcellular access, residence time, and off-target burden, and propose a staged validation workflow from biophysical profiling to locus-specific perturbation. We argue that programmable approaches are valuable complements to, rather than replacements for, optimized small-molecule G4 ligands.

item.title: Discovery of Ebselen Analogs as Novel Inhibitors of Polyphosphate Metabolism to Attenuate Virulence and Show Combination Benefit with Meropenem in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
item.description:
Abstract
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe hospital-acquired infections. The challenge in treating these infections is exacerbated by increasing antibiotic resistance. Polyphosphate kinases (PPKs), specifically PPK1 and PPK2, play a critical role in the virulence, stress response, and antibiotic tolerance of P. aeruginosa, making it a compelling target for therapeutic intervention. In this study, we describe the discovery and development of ebselen analogs as novel inhibitors against PPK1Pa and PPK2Pa. Biochemical and cellular assays revealed that ebselens interfere with the polyphosphate homeostasis within the bacterium. EB-1 and EB-18 treatment significantly reduced intracellular polyP levels, mirroring the phenotypic effects observed in Δppk strains, including impaired biofilm formation, reduced motility, and attenuated production of pyoverdine and pyocyanin. Notably, EB-1 and EB-18 showed combination benefit with meropenem against P. aeruginosa in the Galleria model, supporting their potential as an adjunctive agent to improve the antibacterial efficacy of meropenem. Most representative compounds, including EB-1 and EB-18, showed no detectable cytotoxicity in the tested mammalian cells. These findings underscore ebselen analogs as promising dual-specific PPK inhibitors, establishing a valuable strategy for the development of adjunct therapies via the PPK-mediated anti-virulence pathways.

item.title: Refinement of Peptidomimetics toward MUR-2425: A Brain-Penetrant and Selective Caspase-2 Inhibitor with Enhanced Pharmacokinetics
item.description:
Abstract
Caspase-2 (Casp2) has emerged as a promising target for tau-associated neurodegenerative diseases, yet the development of potent, selective, and drug-like inhibitors remains challenging. Here, we report a systematic structure–activity relationship study of 80 novel covalent-reversible peptidomimetic Casp2 inhibitors, revealing key structural features of the Casp2 S2–S3 binding site and discovering (S)-2-methylindoline-2-carboxylic acid (2-Me-Idc) and quinaldic acid (Quin) as versatile and stable P5 scaffolds. One-step conversion of the aldehyde warhead into a nitrile remarkably enhanced selectivity while maintaning potency. The results culminate in MUR-2425 (87, (2-Me-Idc)(hE)VP*D-CN), a nanomolar Casp2 inhibitor (pKi (cpCasp2) = 7.75) with ≥525-fold selectivity over Casp1/3/4/5/6/7/9/10 and 24-fold over Casp8. MUR-2425 prevents the formation of neurotoxic Δtau314 in vitro, exhibits stable ADMET properties across human, rat, and mouse species and proves brain penetrance after subcutaneous injection in CD-1 mice. MUR-2425 is confirmed to engage Casp2 covalently by cocrystallization, supporting its further development for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias.

item.title: Beyond CRBN and VHL: DCAF16-Recruiting Degraders from Rational Design to Clinical Translation
item.description:
Abstract
Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has revolutionized modern drug discovery. However, the current clinical landscape remains predominantly reliant on CRBN and VHL, restricting the targetable proteome and increasing the risk of acquired resistance. Expanding the TPD toolbox with therapeutically tractable E3 ligases is imperative. Recently, DCAF16 has emerged as a frontrunner in this effort, underscored by the advancement of DCAF16-based monovalent degraders such as PLX-61639 and AMX-883 toward clinical evaluation. Unlike the historically serendipitous discovery of CRBN-based molecular glues, DCAF16 offers a versatile platform for the rational design of both bifunctional and monovalent degraders. In this timely perspective, we present the first comprehensive medicinal chemistry analysis of the DCAF16-mediated degradation landscape, focusing on delineating the expanding diversity of recruiting motifs and elucidating the design principles, structural basis, and SAR of representative degraders. Finally, we outline current challenges and offer insights into future design strategies and clinical translation of DCAF16-based degraders.

item.title: Compact Sulfonyl-γ-AApeptide Foldamers for Targeting Translation Initiation Machinery Assembly
item.description:
Abstract
Dysregulated cap-dependent translation is a hallmark of malignant transformation and progression, yet direct inhibition of the dynamic eIF4E−eIF4G protein−protein interaction remains challenging. Herein, we report the rational design of short helical sulfonyl-γ-AApeptide foldamers mimicking the eIF4G1 α-helical binding motif and directly engaging eIF4E. Structure-guided optimization, including stereochemical remodeling, afforded a compact, right-handed foldamer with remarkable proteolytic stability, submicromolar affinity for eIF4E, and potent inhibition of cap-dependent translation. Recognizing that cancer cells exploit enhanced lysosome-centered signaling and trafficking programs to sustain cap-dependent translation, we repurposed this oncogenic dependency as an intracellular delivery route to release the translation inhibitor. The optimized conjugate suppresses ferritin translation, triggers lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, and exhibits antitumor activity in vivo. Together, these findings establish short sulfonyl-γ-AApeptides as an effective chemical modality for targeting eIF4E−eIF4G interface and demonstrate that dynamic assembly events within the translation initiation machinery can be manipulated through rational foldamer design.

item.title: Identification and Optimization of Novel Dual PARP/Tubulin Colchicine-Binding Site Inhibitors for Cancer Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Dual targeting of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) and the colchicine-binding site (CBS) of tubulin represents a promising strategy to overcome tumor heterogeneity and acquired resistance. Herein, a series of benzofused heterocyclic carboxamide derivatives were designed and synthesized as novel dual PARP/CBS inhibitors. Structure−activity relationship studies identified D13 as the most potent lead, demonstrating low-nanomolar antiproliferative activities (IC50 = 2−15 nM) across multiple cancer cell lines with high selectivity over normal cells. D13 inhibited PARP1/2 enzymatic activity and suppressed tubulin polymerization via CBS binding. D13 also induced G2/M arrest, DNA damage, and apoptosis, while blocking cell migration and tube formation. In an MDA-MB-231 xenograft model, D13 at 20 mg/kg achieved 72.3% tumor growth inhibition with dose-dependent efficacy and good tolerability, outperforming veliparib, phenstatin, and their combination. These findings validate dual PARP/CBS inhibition as a viable therapeutic strategy and support further development of D13 as an anticancer lead.

item.title: Discovery of Quinoline-Based Highly Potent and Selective THRβ Agonists for MASLD Treatment
item.description:
Abstract
Metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a progressive metabolic liver disease lacking sufficient clinical therapies. Thyroid hormone receptor β (THRβ), a liver-enriched nuclear receptor, is an attractive therapeutic target. Resmetirom, the first FDA-approved THRβ agonist for MASH, achieves clinical efficacy yet suffers from suboptimal THRβ/THRα selectivity restricting its therapeutic window. We used a scaffold-hopping strategy to design and synthesize a novel series of quinoline-based THRβ agonists. Systematic SAR optimization identified compound 24 as a potent, selective THRβ agonist, with an EC50 of 46.07 nM and 34.3-fold THRβ/THRα selectivity. It displayed favorable oral bioavailability (F = 54.1%) and approximately 2-fold higher hepatic exposure than Resmetirom. In animal models, compound 24 ameliorated metabolic dysfunction, reduced hepatic lipid accumulation, and suppressed liver inflammation and fibrosis. No obvious thyroid axis disruption or THRα-mediated cardiotoxicity was observed, and mice tolerated compound 24 up to 100 mg/kg. Overall, compound 24 represents a promising THRβ-selective therapeutic candidate for MASH.

item.title: Development of Potent METTL1 Inhibitors Using a Nanoscale Direct-To-Biology Strategy
item.description:
Abstract
The RNA methyltransferase METTL1/WDR4, which catalyzes N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification in tRNA, has emerged as a key regulator of mRNA translation, and its dysregulation is associated with cancer development. Here, we report the development of a potent series of METTL1 inhibitors by combining conventional structure−activity relationship (SAR) studies with a tandem direct-to-biology (D2B) approach. Lead compound VK238 inhibited METTL1 enzymatic activity at nanomolar concentrations and exhibited selectivity across a panel of methyltransferases and kinases. In a cellular context, pharmacological METTL1 inhibition reduced m7G levels in tRNAs, leading to apoptosis-mediated cell death in several acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell lines. Mechanistic studies combining biophysical experiments, photoaffinity labeling (PAL), and molecular docking suggested that this inhibitor series occupies the (S)-adenosylmethionine (SAM) binding pocket of METTL1. Collectively, these findings highlight METTL1 as a tractable and pharmacologically relevant target for therapeutic intervention in AML.
