The representative compound, 26, generated by appending an electrophilic monomethyl fumarate handle to a TTK inhibitor, effectively induced TTK degradation and demonstrated superior antiproliferative activity across diverse cancer cell lines. Mechanistic investigations suggested that compound 26 primarily engages RNF126 and stabilizes its association with TTK, thereby inducing TTK ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Collectively, this work provides the first example of a TTK molecular glue-like degrader and introduces a new electrophilic handle for the rational design of degraders with reduced nonspecific cytotoxicity.

item.title: Discovery of Pyrazolo[1,5- a ]-1,3,5-Triazine Derivatives as Potent, Highly Selective and Orally Available Macrocyclic CDK7 Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclin-dependent kinase 7 (CDK7) is a promising cancer therapeutic target due to its dual role in cell cycle progression and gene transcription. However, current CDK7 inhibitors generally exhibit poor kinase selectivity. Herein, we performed in-depth structural optimization on a 17-membered macrocyclic scaffold, and identified compound I-23, which potently inhibits CDK7 with an IC50 value of 3 nM and exhibits exceptional CDK7 selectivity with no significant off-target activity across 416 kinases. I-23 also potently inhibits cell proliferation across a panel of tumor cell lines, induces cell cycle arrest and transcriptional suppression, and downregulates oncoprotein c-Myc, particularly in triple-negative breast cancer cells. Importantly, I-23 shows favorable oral bioavailability (up to 28%) with linear pharmacokinetics. Collectively, this work provides a highly selective and orally bioavailable macrocyclic CDK7 inhibitor, which can serve as a valuable chemical tool for dissecting CDK7 biological functions and a promising lead compound for CDK7-based anticancer drug discovery.

item.title: Discovery of YKS-34 , a Highly Selective PDE4B Inhibitor for the Treatment of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
item.description:
Abstract
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remains a progressive and fatal lung disease with a substantial unmet need for safe and effective therapies. Highly selective inhibition of phosphodiesterase 4B (PDE4B) represents a promising therapeutic strategy for IPF while avoiding nausea and vomiting associated with PDE4D inhibition. However, achieving pronounced subtype selectivity remains particularly challenging; notably, the only approved PDE4B-preferential inhibitor, nerandomilast, exhibits only approximately 9-fold selectivity for PDE4B over PDE4D. Herein, we report the identification of YKS-34, a potent PDE4B inhibitor (IC50 = 1.71 nM) exhibiting >1000-fold selectivity over PDE4A, PDE4C, and PDE4D. YKS-34 effectively suppressed TGF-β-induced fibroblast activation and LPS-induced TNF-α release in vitro. In vivo, YKS-34 showed favorable pharmacokinetic properties, lung tissue accumulation, and reduced emetic potential at tested conditions while dose-dependently improving pulmonary dysfunction and fibrotic remodeling in a bleomycin-induced IPF mouse model. Consequently, YKS-34 emerges as a highly promising, next-generation candidate for the treatment of IPF.

item.title: Design and Synthesis of Novel, Non-ATP-Competitive MKK3 Modulators as Suppressors of TNF-α Production for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis
item.description:
Abstract
Although TNF-α is a clinically validated target for Ulcerative colitis (UC), therapy is dominated by injectable biologics, with no oral small-molecule inhibitors approved. Traditional ATP-competitive p38 inhibitors designed to regulate TNF-α have failed in clinical trials due to poor kinome selectivity. As the primary upstream activator of p38, MKK3 is considered a promising alternative target, but the development of small molecules remains limited, with a notable absence of non-ATP-competitive modulators. Herein, we report a series of compounds targeting the non-ATP-competitive pocket of MKK3 to suppress TNF-α production. Among them, (R)-48 was identified as a lead candidate, demonstrating robust suppression of TNF-α (IC50: 0.038 μM), high oral bioavailability (62.6%), clear dose-dependent efficacy and strong PK/PD relationships in mouse UC models. Particularly, HDX-MS suggested (R)-48 probably binds to a distal allosteric site on MKK3, precluding TAK1-mediated activation. Altogether, (R)-48 emerges as a promising oral small-molecule therapeutic candidate for the treatment of UC.

item.title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of Six-Transmembrane Epithelial Antigen of Prostate 2 Targeted PET Probes: A Case of Drug Repurposing Based on Molecular Docking
item.description:
Abstract
Six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate 2 (STEAP2) is overexpressed in prostate cancer, yet no STEAP2-targeted imaging probes exist. Using molecular docking, we screened triptorelin and leuprorelin by radioiodine labeling and identified triptorelin as a high-affinity, selective ligand. To enhance in vivo stability and pharmacokinetics, triptorelin underwent acetylation, PEG extension, and 4-iodophenylbutyric acid conjugation, yielding five DOTA-conjugated analogs radiolabeled with 68Ga. In 22Rv1 xenografts, 68Ga-Trip-5 exhibited moderate but specific tumor uptake (SUVmax 1.8) with favorable tumor-to-background contrast. In vivo stability, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, and human radiation dosimetry (effective dose 0.00345 mSv/MBq) demonstrated favorable safety. Autoradiography on human prostate cancer specimens showed probe accumulation correlating with endogenous STEAP2 expression. This represents the first STEAP2-targeted PET probe developed via molecular docking-guided drug repurposing. Cellular, biochemical, and imaging data provide supportive evidence of STEAP2-mediated targeting. Preclinical performance supports clinical translation of 68Ga-Trip-5, with definitive target validation

item.title: Synthesis and In Vitro/In Vivo Stability Evaluation of Various Radioiodinated Tyrosine Derivatives
item.description:
Abstract
Radioiodinated drugs face limited application due to severe in vivo deiodination. In this study, nine tyrosine derivatives were synthesized and evaluated to develop stable radioiodinated prosthetic groups to reduce deiodination. Biodistribution results revealed that replacing phenolic hydroxyl and amino groups with methoxy and acetamide groups enhanced stability. Compound 131I-8 exhibited the highest stability, with a maximum thyroid uptake of 1.13 ± 0.12 %ID (approximately one-20th of 131I-Tyr). It’s high stability was explained by in vitro stability experiments and molecular docking. A new PSMA-targeted radioiodinated drug, [125/131I]IMPA, was synthesized to verify whether compound 8 remained stable after conjugation with drugs. It exhibited a lower thyroid uptake of only 0.19 ± 0.03 %ID, approximately 100-fold lower than that of the control compound [131I]ITPA, which has a tyrosine moiety as the radioiodination site. In conclusion, 8 is a small, easily labeled, and highly stable prosthetic group with promising potential for developing stable radioiodinated drugs and broadening their therapeutic application.

item.title: Discovery of Neurolysin Activators with Preclinical Efficacy in an Ischemic Stroke Model
item.description:
Abstract
The peptidase neurolysin (Nln) is upregulated following ischemic stroke to activate endogenous cerebroprotective mechanisms and has subsequently emerged as a therapeutic target for drug discovery efforts. Overexpression of Nln in a mouse model of ischemic stroke results in significant improvement of stroke outcomes. Herein, we report the discovery of the first non-peptide Nln activators based around a central pyridine-piperazine scaffold that possesses nanomolar potency. This scaffold, exemplified by compounds 7c and 7g, exhibits greater in vitro half-life, blood−brain barrier penetration, mouse brain and mouse plasma stability than previously reported peptidomimetic Nln activators. Compound 7g afforded an in vivo protective effect in the MCAO mouse model of ischemic stroke, significantly reducing infarct volume and brain water content, marking the first report of a small molecule Nln activator with in vivo cerebroprotective effects in a preclinical model.

item.title: Discovery and Optimization of Indole-Based CDK9 Inhibitors for Hepatocellular Carcinoma
item.description:
Abstract
CDK9 has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for anticancer drug development. Although multiple CDK9 inhibitors have entered clinical evaluation, differentiated scaffolds with convincing activity and tolerability in solid tumors remain limited. In this study, we identified a series of indole-based CDK9 inhibitors through virtual screening and structure-based drug design, and systematically evaluated their therapeutic potential in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Among these compounds, W24 exhibited potent CDK9 inhibitory activity (IC50 = 0.9 nM) and a preliminary kinase selectivity profile. W24 effectively induced HCC cell death in vitro, which was accompanied by DNA damage and downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Mcl-1. Furthermore, W24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in HepG2 and Huh-7 xenograft models with an acceptable safety profile under the tested dosing regimen. Collectively, these findings highlight W24 as a promising lead compound and provide valuable insights for the development of next-generation CDK9 inhibitors for the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma.

item.title: Lung-Tailored Pyrrolo-pyrimidine DDR Inhibitors Designed for Optimized Local Delivery
item.description:
Abstract
Preclinical studies highlighted the key role of Discoidin Domain Receptors (DDRs) in fibrotic processes, making them promising targets for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) treatment. In this work, we describe the design of a novel class of DDR inhibitors and their subsequent optimization toward inhaled delivery. Following a structure-based approach, we identified two chemical series based on 5:6 heterocyclic cores showing nanomolar affinity for DDR1 and DDR2 and a promising kinome selectivity profile. An inhaled-by-design medchem strategy was then applied to optimize potency, phys-chem, and in vitro ADME properties, tailored to achieve lung-restricted compounds. This effort resulted in the discovery of compound 25, a novel and highly potent DDR inhibitor that combined antifibrotic activity in a TGFβ-induced in vitro fibrosis model with an outstanding pharmacokinetic profile and the desired lung-targeted behavior following inhaled administration.

item.title: Design and Biological Evaluation of FAP-Man, a Mannosylated FAP-Targeted Radioglycopeptide for Tumor Imaging and Radionuclide Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is an attractive target for radiotheranostic development because of its abundant expression in tumor-associated fibroblasts and limited distribution in normal tissues. Here, we developed FAP-Man, a mannosylated FAP-targeted radioglycopeptide based on the FAP-2286 scaffold, to optimize tumor targeting and pharmacokinetic properties. Compared with [68Ga]Ga-FAP-2286, [68Ga]Ga-FAP-Man showed higher tumor uptake in U87MG tumor-bearing mice (16.917 ± 4.986 vs 3.188 ± 0.535 %ID/g at 1 h post-injection) and improved tumor-to-liver contrast. Both [177Lu]Lu-FAP-Man and [225Ac]Ac-FAP-Man significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with PBS-treated controls. Preliminary clinical PET imaging further supported its potential for favorable lesion visualization and lesion-to-background contrast, particularly for hepatic lesions. These findings support further evaluation of FAP-Man as a FAP-targeted radiopharmaceutical candidate.
